GoalInput.description:
An owner's completion condition for one conversation.

``max_rounds`` is **tri-state**, and the three states mean three different
things. Omitted — the ordinary case, and what every client sends — leaves
whatever bound the goal already carries exactly as it is, so a caller that
only changes the words cannot silently delete a limit its owner stated.
A number states a bound; an explicit ``null`` lifts one. That is why no
writer reads the field directly: what the request *said* is
:attr:`states_max_rounds`, and absence is not the same fact as ``None``.

max_rounds.description: An explicit maximum number of automatic rounds. A number sets it and an explicit null lifts it; omitting the field leaves whatever bound the goal already carries unchanged. Omitting it on a goal that has none means no limit: the goal continues until the objective is met, paused, cleared, blocked on the owner, or stopped by an existing run-time limit. There is no default and no maximum.
max_rounds.title: Max Rounds

GoalInput.title: GoalInput

GoalLimits.description:
Advertise the server's goal bounds to clients before they submit.

Only the objective is bounded. There is no advertised round ceiling and no
advertised default, because there is neither: a client that wants a bound
states one, and a client that does not leaves the field out. Advertising a
number here is what made "unlimited" look like "fifty" to every reader.
GoalLimits.title: GoalLimits

GoalRequest.description:
A goal write, with the revision the caller read it at.

``revision`` is what makes two edits from two tabs resolvable: the second
one is refused rather than silently overwriting the first. Omitted means
"write it whatever it currently says", which is what a first-time set from
the composer wants.
GoalRequest.title: GoalRequest

GoalResponse.description:
The conversation's goal after a write that changed it.

Answered from the *thread*, not from a turn: a goal belongs to the
conversation, and a conversation whose newest turn has been deleted still
has one. ``revision`` is echoed even when there is no goal, so a client can
compare and set without a separate read.
GoalResponse.title: GoalResponse

GoalRevisionRequest.description:
An optional compare-and-set guard on a goal operation.

Omitted means "act on whatever the goal currently is", which is what the
pause and resume buttons send: they are idempotent by nature, and refusing
to press one because a round advanced a counter would be a worse answer than
doing what was asked.
GoalRevisionRequest.title: GoalRevisionRequest

``storage`` is absent as well as null on a runner that predates the
sub-block: silence about a capability that does not exist is not the same
statement as a runner that has the capability and reported a gap, and the
admin view is where those two are told apart (``not_reported``).

HostCapacityReport.description:
One host-capacity observation, exactly as a runner reports it.

Every rule here is about not letting an unavailable measurement be mistaken
for a real one. A null CPU percentage carries the reason it is null; a
missing ``MemAvailable`` produces no memory figure at all rather than
falling back to ``MemFree``, which answers a different question; and a host
whose boot id could not be read reports neither CPU nor memory, because
without it two machines' numbers are indistinguishable.

HostCapacityStorage.description:
The filesystem that holds sandbox writable layers, as one runner read it.

Block space in the ``df`` sense: ``total`` is the filesystem's size,
``free`` includes the blocks reserved for root, ``available`` excludes
them. All three are kept because the percentage is taken over
``used + available`` — collapsing ``free`` into ``total - available`` would
report every healthy filesystem as partly full with blocks nobody wrote.

Strict integers on purpose: a JSON ``true`` or ``"1024"`` coerced to a
number would put a figure on an operator's screen that no machine ever
measured, and the coercion is invisible by the time it is rendered.

source.description: Identifier of the method that produced the reading, e.g. 'linux_overlay_root_statvfs'. Deliberately not an enum: a new probe must not require a control-plane release, and the page never branches on this value.

The sum over every tracked work thread of its ``se.sum_exec_runtime``
delta. A thread that ran on two cores for ten seconds contributes about
twenty seconds, so this may legitimately exceed wall-clock duration.
Never derived from a utilisation percentage, and never summed from tool
rows in place of the whole turn.

TurnMemoryResources.description:
The sampled peak of the member's proportional resident memory.

``peak_bytes`` is the maximum over census cycles of the sum of PSS across
the member's distinct address spaces. PSS shares mapped resident pages
between users instead of billing each of them in full, but it is not
machine memory: it excludes the VM kernel, unmapped page cache, host
services and special page classes, and RSS is never substituted for it.
Sampling cannot see between ticks, so even a complete plan stays labelled
``sampled``.

TurnResourceSummary.description:

Derived from the stored snapshot rather than recomputed: the list view, the
detail view and any later aggregation share one reducer. ``state`` is
derived too — a stored ``collecting`` snapshot for an attempt that is
already terminal reads as ``interrupted``, with ``observed_through_ms``
kept so the UI can say how far it actually got instead of rounding it up
to the end of the task.

TurnStorageIoResources.description:

byte is attributed. ``rchar``/``wchar`` are deliberately absent — they
count pipes, sockets and terminals too, so they cannot stand in for
storage I/O.

put.description:
Pin new chat placement to one host, or let any host materialize it.

Non-preemptive, and worth being precise about: the new host starts claiming
new chats at once, while jobs already running on the old one keep running to
the end. Existing retained chats also remain hard-pinned to their owning
host for later follow-ups because their Docker writable layer is not
portable in this phase. The two hosts can therefore overlap. This is not a
drain, which would mean waiting for the old host to empty before the new one
starts.

post.description:
Mint a one-time token that lets one named machine join the pool.

Returned in full here and **nowhere else** — only its hash is stored, so
there is no endpoint that can show it again and no database read that can
recover it. An operator who loses it issues another.

**The token names its host, and the caller here is the one who names it.**
It did not, once, and the name was therefore whatever the registering
machine typed — while registration upserts, so a name that already belongs
to a live host revokes that host's credential and drops it back to
``enrolling``. A mistyped name evicted a working, busy machine from the
claim pool. Refusing names already in use was the other candidate, but it
breaks the case the upsert exists for (a rebuilt machine coming back under
its own name) and leaves the naming decision on the unauthenticated side
anyway. Registration always needs a freshly minted token, so binding the
name costs the operator nothing and moves the decision to the party this
endpoint has already authenticated.

The TTL stays short for the reason it always was: the window is one
machine, once, for as long as it takes to finish a setup already under way.

delete.description:
Drop a decommissioned host from the list.

Housekeeping only: a runner still polling on that machine re-adds itself
within seconds. The active host cannot be dropped, because doing so would
silently unpin new-chat placement, which is the opposite of what removing a
host from a list looks like it does. Existing retained owners are not moved
by forgetting their pool row; their broker routing continues to fail closed
until the same named host is enrolled again. The active-host refusal is
decided inside the store's transaction, not by a check here: a check here
is a read a concurrent switch can outrun.

get.description:
Read one host's stored CPU and memory history.

Separate from the pool endpoint on purpose. The table is the page's main
information and it loads on every poll; a 24-hour curve is wanted only when
an operator opens one machine, and folding it into the poll would make
every thirty seconds cost a day of rows per host.

Only the current epoch is served. A rebuilt machine inherits its name, so
an older generation's points describe hardware that is no longer there —
the response carries the epoch so a client can tell that its curve is
stale rather than let it appear to continue into the new machine.

Every point is one observation of one minute, and a minute nobody measured
comes back as an explicit null rather than as an interpolated value: the
chart exists to show when a machine was in trouble, and a filled-in gap is
the one thing that would hide it.

post.description:
Stop this host taking new work; let what it has finish.

The counterpart to the pin, and the thing the pin is not: switching moves
new claims elsewhere *and* leaves the old host running its jobs with no way
to tell when it is empty. Draining is the same first half plus a slot
counter that walks down to zero, which is the number ``remove`` refuses to
act before.

Revoke this host's credential and take it out of the pool.

Refused while the host still holds slots, unless forced. The refusal is not
bureaucracy: the running attempts belong to a machine the platform has just
declared gone, and nobody would learn that until their leases lapsed
minutes later. Being told "it is still busy" is the difference between
draining first and finding out afterwards.

Forced removal is the deliberate version of the same thing. Lease fencing
rejects later writes from the superseded worker. A retained activation is
not replayed because the platform cannot know whether its prompt ran, so
that chat is marked LOST when the lease expires.

The row survives, disabled. ``agent_attempts.host_id`` points at it, and
"where did this job run" should not become unanswerable because the machine
was retired. ``DELETE`` forgets that administrative row; neither action is
evidence that the retained container or Docker data-root was deleted.

put.description:
Set or clear runtime settings for one server, over the global values.

A value set here wins over the one set for every server. ``null`` clears
it, and the server goes back to the global value, or the built-in default when there
is none. Applied from the host's next heartbeat, like the global values,
and kept through heartbeats and re-enrollment.

Ask one host to run this many turns at once, without touching its deployment.

The host runs one long-lived service and starts a process per turn as it
claims one, so this is a limit rather than a fleet size: nothing is started
or stopped when it changes. The host reads it off its next heartbeat answer
and serves it from then on, reporting it back as ``slots_total``.

The claim admits against the lower of the requested and reported numbers.
Lowering therefore takes effect immediately, before the host has even heard
about it, and turns already running are untouched — they finish, and the
host simply claims nothing more until it is under the new limit. Raising
takes effect when the host confirms, which is one heartbeat away.

**Saving is not applying.** This stores the number and says so; the page
shows whether the host has confirmed it, and says when a host is offline or
when its runner predates remote sizing and needs a redeploy to change.
``null`` returns the host to its own ``AGENT_HOST_SLOTS`` default.

is the safe thing to try first.

post.description:
Report liveness, and whatever about this machine has changed.

Promotes ``enrolling`` and ``offline`` hosts to ``online``: a machine that
comes back from a partition needs no operator to put it back to work.
Deliberately does **not** promote a ``draining`` one — a heartbeat says "I
am here", not "I should be taking work" — and a ``disabled`` host cannot
get this far, because its credential no longer authenticates.

Spend a one-time enrollment token and receive a host credential.

The token is consumed before the credential is minted, and both happen
before the response is written — so a machine that crashes mid-registration
has burnt its token and needs a new one. That is the right way round: the
alternative leaves a token that looks unused but may have already produced
a credential.

The host starts at ``enrolling`` and claims nothing until it heartbeats.
A machine that registers and never comes up therefore never receives work,
which is the difference between a pool entry and a promise.

``name`` is checked against the name the token was issued for, inside the
same statement that spends it. Registration upserts, so a name already held
by a live host loses its credential and drops back to ``enrolling``; before
the binding, one typo here evicted a working machine from the pool. A
mismatch does not consume the token, so a typo is retried rather than
re-issued.

Return the profiling policy this host must apply.

A dedicated read so a Start or a Stop reaches a host that is between beats.
It takes the same credential the beat does, so the host needs no second
secret, and the sandbox -- which never holds the credential -- can reach
nothing here.

The host is resolved by the credential and never named by the request, which
is what makes it impossible to ask about another machine: an answer is
computed for whoever authenticated.

delete.description:
Remove the goal, and every automatic round that was queued for it.

The revision moves and the identity is cleared, so a report written about
the removed objective can never match whatever the owner sets next.

get.description:
The conversation's goal, or the fact that it has none.

Answered from the thread rather than from a turn, and answered with the
*control revision* even when there is no goal: that revision is what the
next write's ``expected_revision`` is compared against, so a client can
create the first goal on a conversation it just read without a second
round trip.

put.description:
Create, replace or edit the conversation's completion condition.

A new objective is a new authorization: it mints a new goal identity, starts
the round count over, and becomes active. Editing the bound of an active
goal leaves the identity and the rounds spent alone; editing a paused one
leaves it paused, because changing the words is not resuming it.

``max_rounds`` is the owner's own bound and is *optional*: omitted — what
every client sends — means the goal runs until it is finished, stopped,
cleared, blocked on the owner, or an existing run-time limit applies. There
is no default and no maximum. An explicit value is honored exactly, and is
distinguishable from its absence because absence is ``null``, never a large
integer.

``revision`` is what makes two edits from two tabs resolvable — the second is
refused with a 409 rather than silently overwriting the first. Omitted means
"write it whatever it currently says", which is what a first set wants.

post.description:
Stop the goal continuing itself; leave the turn that is already running.

Queued automatic rounds are cancelled with it, so a round the goal asked for
cannot start after the owner stopped it. A *running* round is deliberately
left alone: "stop after this turn" and "stop this turn" are different
requests, and the second one is the existing stop button.

Start a paused goal moving again, and record the obligation to schedule.

The owner's authorization is the trigger: no model report is needed to start
working again, and the wakeup this writes is what makes the next round
happen — the request does not wait for it, and does not need to.

A goal that paused because it reached a bound the *owner* set is resumed
without that bound, and the response says so: ``max_rounds`` comes back
``null``. Refusing instead would leave the only Resume control in the
product pointing at a state nothing can clear — the round bound has no
configuration surface — which is the dead end this endpoint exists to
remove.

get.description:
The conversation's waiting messages and its newest turn, without the transcript.

The page reads this while messages wait: when the newest turn changes to
one of them, it has been sent.

post.description:
Send a message: the next turn now if nothing is running, otherwise queued.

Every message goes through here. It is checked against the conversation's
newest turn — the same checks a follow-up always passed — and put at the end
of the thread's queue; the queue is then settled, which on an idle
conversation makes it the next turn before this returns (``job``). With a
turn running it waits (``pending``) and is sent, in order, when that turn
ends. Sending on an idle conversation whose queue was paused is the owner
continuing: older waiting messages go first.

An ``Idempotency-Key`` names this one submission. A resend answers with what
the first send made — the turn if it has become one, the waiting message if
not — and the same key under different content is a 409
``idempotency_conflict``.

``require_idle`` binds a fresh action to ``expected_latest_job_id`` and
refuses it with ``conversation_changed`` if any chat sharing the workspace
has a live turn or waiting message, a Fork is active, or the workspace is
unpublished at the locked write. An accepted idle-only action creates its
turn in that same transaction without entering the pending queue.

delete.description:
Withdraw a waiting message, at the revision the caller read.

Its uploads go back to being staged. A stale ``revision`` is a 409
``revision_conflict`` carrying the message as it is now.

patch.description:
Change a waiting message, at the revision the caller read.

Only the fields sent change. ``state: held`` is how an editor stops the
queue at this message while it is being rewritten; ``state: queued`` lets
it go again. A stale ``revision`` is a 409 ``revision_conflict`` carrying
the message as it is now.

post.description:
Send one waiting message into the live turn.

The owner's choice, kept: the message goes in front of the model before
its next tool call, and joins the transcript where the turn's own stream
says the turn took it. Until then it is ``sending``. A turn no host has
taken yet is given it once one has. A turn that answers without another
tool call never takes it, and it goes as the next turn, as any waiting
message does. A turn that cannot have it at all — its host is out of
reach, or it just ended — leaves it waiting where it was, and
``not_delivered_reason`` says why. With nothing live, this is an ordinary
send.

post.description: Answer only the native request belonging to the attempt the owner saw.

Continue a paused queue from its first message.

The pause is cleared and, when nothing is running, the ending that caused
it counts as seen, so the queue does not stop again for the same turn. The
queue is then settled: on an idle conversation its first message becomes
the next turn before this returns (``job``).

Only a staged one: once a turn has accepted a file, the turn owns it, and
deleting the conversation is what removes the bytes.

Claim the next queued job and mint this attempt's capability token.

Returns ``null`` (HTTP 200) when the queue is empty, and equally when an
operator has pinned agent jobs to a different host than the one this runner
reports. The two are deliberately the same answer on the wire: a runner
that has been switched away from should idle exactly as it does when there
is no work, not treat it as an error worth retrying differently. Which host
is active is an admin question, answered on the admin surface.

**Enrolled-host only.** ``claim_job`` takes the oldest queued job across all
tenants, and the response carries that job's repo, prompt, and metadata
plus a working capability token for it — so ordinary API-key auth here
would let any customer dequeue and read another customer's job, and drain
the queue besides.

The per-host credential opens registration/heartbeat/claim surfaces and
never enters the sandbox; only the returned per-attempt tokens go in.

get.description:
List every upload in this conversation, so /uploads can be rebuilt.

Scoped to the thread rather than the claimed turn: a retry on a fresh
container has to restore all of them, and re-importing into a retained one
simply overwrites the same paths.

Read one upload's bytes for the host that is running this turn.

The thread from the worker token's own job is what scopes the read, so a

post.description:
Record which continuity rung this attempt runs on (design §9).

Observability, deliberately fenced like every other worker write: a
superseded attempt must not be able to relabel how the live one ran.
Append one normalized event to the job's append-only log.

Drive the fenced terminal transition for this attempt.

Then, before acknowledging, act on what the ending means for the rest of
the conversation: the owner's waiting messages first, then the goal.

Takes the source-control runtime rather than the App's credentials: a turn
that finished is recorded and acknowledged whether or not the App can be
loaded right now (issue #47). Only sending the next waiting message and the
next goal round wait for it.
Renew the attempt's lease and learn about pending cancellation.
Store one finished measurement without requiring a still-live lease.

Hand a claimed turn back to the queue, having never started it.

The one path from a claim back to ``queued`` without spending an attempt.
A host claims a turn and then starts the process that will run it; when
that process cannot be started, or exits without taking delivery, the turn
has provably not begun and the person waiting on it should not wait out a
lease that nothing is holding.

A short retry delay lets other queued work proceed while the host recovers
from a temporary refusal, including work that can resume an existing sandbox.

**Not an escape hatch for a turn that is running.** The release is refused
once the turn has been admitted to the CLI, and the check is the database's
rather than the caller's: replaying an admitted prompt executes the same
instruction twice, which is what the retained-session rules exist to
prevent. A caller that is refused has lost nothing — the lease was always
the backstop, and it still is.

Record one closed attempt's resource and timing telemetry.

Fenced like every other worker write, and idempotent: the rollup
describes an attempt that is already closed, so a retried post is the same
report said twice rather than a second report to add.
Release a failed activation; ambiguous admission becomes LOST.
Persist at-most-once admission before the prompt reaches the CLI.
Fence and record a replacement Agent CLI process generation.
Reserve immutable one-chat/one-container identity before Docker create.
Mint the renewable member grant before the supervisor opens a CLI.
Confirm the exact retained container reached RUNNING.
Persist the native context boundary before arming idle deactivation.
Resume retained PTYs, then atomically publish workspace readiness.
Fence terminal writes, then freeze retained PTYs for a protected phase.

Record one cumulative whole-turn member execution window.

A separate report from the legacy resource rollup, with its own semantics:
it is cumulative rather than a closed window, so the same snapshot can
arrive more than once while ``report_seq`` stays the only thing that
orders it. ``stored`` and ``duplicate`` are both success — an acknowledged
checkpoint whose response was lost must be safe to resend unchanged.

The body is bounded before it is parsed. The contract caps one summary at
16 KiB of UTF-8, and a rejected oversize report has to be cheap to reject;
letting the model build first would let an unbounded body allocate before
the bound is ever checked. Measuring the raw body is also the only check
that counts what actually crossed the wire rather than what survived
parsing.

Identity comes from the signed claims only. The body cannot name an
attempt, a lease, or a job, so a snapshot can never be filed against
anything but the caller's own fenced attempt.

Hold an idle host's request until there may be work, then answer.

A host whose claim found nothing asks here instead of sleeping out its poll
interval, and claims again when this answers: at once if the token it
passes is stale, when a job is queued, requeued or ends, or after
``timeout_seconds`` regardless. The answer is the token for its next wait
and never a job; the claim stays the only way to take one.

Enrolled hosts only, like the claim it precedes. 404 where nothing listens
for work, which is also what a control plane predating this answers, so a
host treats both the same way and polls.
Record the node's host keys once; repeating the same keys is harmless.
